content: Natural selection is the primary mechanism of evolution, where organisms with heritable traits better suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more successfully. This process requires three key conditions: variation (individuals differ in traits), heritability (traits can be passed to offspring), and differential reproduction (some traits increase survival and reproductive success). Genetic variation arises through mutations (random changes in DNA) and genetic recombination during sexual reproduction, creating the raw material for selection. When environmental pressures act on this variation, individuals with advantageous traits survive at higher ratesâa process called survival of the fittest  where "fitness" means reproductive success rather than physical strength. Over generations, beneficial alleles (gene variants) increase in frequency within the population, while detrimental alleles decrease. This gradual accumulation of favorable traits leads to adaptationâthe process by which populations become better suited to their environments. Different selection modes include directional selection (favoring one extreme of a trait), stabilizing selection (favoring intermediate traits), and disruptive selection (favoring both extremes). Natural selection doesn't create perfect organisms but works with available genetic variation to produce "good enough" solutions that enable survival and reproduction in specific environments."

scenario.title: Evolution Arena
scenario.content: Students create and manage populations of virtual game characters that compete for resources in changing environments. Each character has a genotype (underlying genetic code) that determines its phenotype (visible traits and abilities). Players observe how random mutations and recombination generate variation within their population. As environmental conditions changeâthrough seasons, natural disasters, predator introductions, or resource fluctuationsâdifferent traits become advantageous or disadvantageous. The simulation tracks allele frequencies, population size, and fitness metrics across generations, visualizing evolutionary trends in real-time. Students can isolate variables to test hypotheses about selection pressures or allow complex interactions to emerge. Advanced features demonstrate concepts like genetic drift, gene flow, speciation, and co-evolution, showing how natural selection interacts with other evolutionary mechanisms.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze how natural selection shapes populations by examining the relationship between environmental pressures and trait frequencies over generations. They will predict population changes in response to selective forces and explain how random variation combines with non-random selection to drive adaptive evolution.
